e.etymology: In American use a feminine form of Randy, the pet form of Randall and Randolph, or a pet form of Miranda. In Norway it is a separate name, a contraction of Old Norse Ragnfrid, 'beautiful counsel'.
e.note: Randi is a vulgar word for a prostitute in Hindi and Urdu, and randy is British slang for lustful.

e.etymology: A variant of Mervyn, the English form of Welsh Merfyn, the name of a 9th-century king of Gwynedd. The meaning of the Welsh name is uncertain.
A spelling of Kaylin, a modern American name that joins Kay with the -lyn ending. Some link it to Irish cailin, 'girl', though that word is not used as a name in Ireland.
From the English and Scottish surname meaning 'son of Thom', a short form of Thomas, which comes from Aramaic for 'twin'.

assoc.t: Thompson submachine gun, the Tommy gun

e.etymology: A combination of Lilly, from the lily flower, and Ann, from Hebrew Channah, 'grace'. It is also heard as a spelling of Lillian.
A modern American coinage built on Jay, close in sound to Jayden, Javon and Javen.
From the English word for the clear blue of the sky, which came through Old French azur and Arabic lazaward from the Persian name of the blue stone lapis lazuli.
From an English surname taken from a place in northwest England. In the US it is chosen largely for Wrigley Field, the Chicago Cubs ballpark named for chewing-gum maker William Wrigley Jr.

assoc.t: Wrigley Field, home of the Chicago Cubs

e.etymology: A respelling of Whitley, an English surname and place name from Old English hwit, 'white', and leah, 'woodland clearing'.
A feminine respelling of Ellison, an English surname meaning 'son of Ellis'. Ellis is a medieval English form of Elias (Elijah).
A modern American name that joins Mae with the -leigh ending. Mae is a form of May, a pet form of Mary and Margaret that is also tied to the month.
The Spanish word for money, from Latin denarius, a Roman silver coin. Its use as a first name is recent and American, in the vein of Cash and Legend.

assoc.t: dinero, Spanish and American slang for money

e.note: It is the everyday Spanish word for money, and Spanish speakers will hear it that way.

e.etymology: A respelling of Bexley, an English place name from Old English byxe, 'box tree', and leah, 'clearing'. Bexley is a borough of London and a suburb of Columbus, Ohio.
A spelling of Wren, the small brown songbird, from Old English wrenna. Wrenn is also an old English surname that began as a nickname for a small, lively person.
An anglicized form of Irish Fionnan, a diminutive of fionn, 'fair' or 'white'. Several early Irish saints bore it, among them Saint Finan of Lindisfarne.
From the Germanic elements hari, 'army', and man, 'man'. The Normans brought it to England, and it was revived in the 19th century, partly by German immigrants to America.
namesakes: Herman Munster (father in the sitcom The Munsters)

assoc.t: Pee-wee Herman, Paul Reubens's comic character
Herman Munster of the sitcom The Munsters

e.etymology: A pet form of Frances that became a given name of its own in the 19th century. Frances comes through Old French from Late Latin Franciscus, 'Frankish' or 'French'.
namesakes: Fannie Flagg (author of Fried Green Tomatoes)

assoc.t: Fannie Mae, the US mortgage finance giant

e.note: Sounds like fanny: mild American slang for the backside and a vulgar word in British English.

e.etymology: The short form of Peter, from Greek petros, 'rock', the name Jesus gave the apostle Simon.

assoc.t: for Pete's sake, a mild exclamation
Pete the Cat, children's picture-book character

e.etymology: A spelling of Jaylen, a modern American name built on Jay. The form Jalen was coined in 1973 for basketball player Jalen Rose from the names of his father James and uncle Leonard.
From the surname of Saint Jean-Marie Vianney, the 19th-century French priest known as the Cure of Ars and patron of parish priests. It became a girls' name in Mexico.
The Hebrew form of Jonathan, a shortening of Yehonatan, 'the Lord has given'. In the Bible Jonathan is the son of King Saul and the close friend of David.
From Arabic sa'd, 'good fortune', from the verb sa'ada, 'to be happy or lucky'. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
e.note: English speakers may read it as the word sad.

e.etymology: A spelling of Ibrahim, the Arabic form of Abraham, the patriarch honored in Islam, Judaism and Christianity. Genesis explains the Hebrew name as 'father of a multitude'.
The Polish spelling of Titus, a Roman first name of uncertain, possibly Sabine, origin. Titus was a companion of Saint Paul and the name of a first-century Roman emperor.
A Latin American spelling of Cristian, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'. The added h is widespread in South America.
From the Morrigan, the Irish goddess of battle and fate who often appears as a crow. The Old Irish name is read as 'great queen' or 'phantom queen'.

assoc.t: the Morrigan, Irish goddess of war and fate
Morrigan, the witch in the Dragon Age video games
Morrigan Crow, heroine of the Nevermoor novels

e.etymology: A respelling of Finley, from the Scottish Gaelic name Fionnlagh, built from fionn, 'fair', and laoch, 'warrior'.
A spelling of Liana, a short form of names ending in -liana such as Juliana and Liliana.
A pet form of Bluma, said Blima in the Yiddish of many Hasidic communities, from blum, 'flower'. It is used mainly in Hasidic Jewish families.
e.note: Close to blimey, the British exclamation of surprise.

e.etymology: In American use mostly a spelling of Isa, the Arabic name of Jesus in the Quran. Esa is also a Finnish name, a medieval short form of Esaias (Isaiah).
The French word for sky and heaven, from Latin caelum. As a boys' name it is known from Ciel Phantomhive, the young earl of the manga and anime Black Butler.

assoc.t: Ciel Phantomhive of the manga and anime Black Butler
